Eh, strongly disagree. This guy focuses a lot on the story and setting, the magic system, the active time battle system. He almost completely ignores the state of CRPGs, and where things were on PC and Console at the time.

Which is to say, CRPGs were "dead". Western RPGs were very dormant, and there were some Japanese RPGs that were getting localized, but mostly still utilizing SNES style graphics, even on the PS1. Think about Final Fantasy Tactics, which was a PS1 game.

1997 actually had two landmark RPGs which permanently made their mark. Diablo, and Final Fantasy VII.

When I played Final Fantasy VII for the first time in 1997, I had never seen anything like it. The 3d graphics, the pre-rendered backgrounds, the full motion video. They absolutely blew me away. And then there was the abundance of post game content. Optional boss fights, ultimate equipment and spells to find. Secret characters to unlock. It was a remarkable re-imagining of what an Eastern RPG could be, and for me it had little to nothing to do with the story.

Diablo of course almost permanently dragged Western RPGs into a real time, action oriented paradigm. Dungeons & Dragons went from being turn based and tactical in the Gold Box Games (1988-1993) to real time in the Infinity Engine games (1998-2002), a change I'm not sure was for the better. And it's with us still as more games pay homage to the Infinity Engine and the Gold Box Games.

It was good, not great.

Simplest explanation is the huge marketing campaign (Sony and Square spent double on marketing than they did on development). Nintendo platforms to this date were the place to be for JRPGs, so there was mindshare that needed to be changed. In the process, a lot of RPG newbies decided to give it a shot. Being a good game, they became fans.

Unfortunately, the success of 7 lead to making it the standard, leading to 8 being what it was, followed by an overcorrection in 9, and the magic of what makes each Final Fantasy game special died.
